notes:
**Scope note.** I ran three searches. They covered Gallup approval series, Census and EAC turnout data, and Gallup/Brookings material on incumbents. I found nothing reliable on three things:
- Evidence by nativity or citizenship.
- Evidence by region (Northeast, Midwest, South, border, West).
- Studies of the "no pandemic" counterfactual itself.

Most of the evidence below is national or by party, sex or race. Where a group breakdown is missing, I say so.

## 1. Direct evidence: Trump's standing before and after the pandemic

**Overall approval**
- Trump's approval peaked at 49% several times in early 2020, between the Senate impeachment trial and the early stage of the pandemic, when Americans gave him high marks for his response. [S1]
- It then fell from 49% in May to 39% in the Gallup poll of May 28–June 4. [S4]
- That fall coincided with the George Floyd protests, so the drop can't be assigned to COVID alone. Gallup attributes it to the racial-justice protests and growing displeasure with his pandemic handling. [S1]
- Approval then sat in the 38–42% range over the summer. [S5]
- It reached 46% in the two weeks before the first debate. [S5]
- His final preelection rating was 46%, the highest for any defeated incumbent in Gallup's record. [S24]

**Economy**
- Trump started 2020 with the highest economic approval of any president seeking reelection since Gallup began the current format under Reagan. [S8]
- His economic approval was 63% in January, before the recession. It was 48% in August, down 15 points. [S2]
- Gallup's Economic Confidence Index fell from +40 in January to −21 in late May/early June. [S8]
- Gallup noted that the recession was caused by a pandemic, which at least partly shielded Trump from blame. [S8]

**Handling of the pandemic**
- Approval of his coronavirus response fell 24 points from March. [S2]
- It went from 60% in March to 36% in August. [S2]

**By group (party only)**
- From March to April, approval of his coronavirus handling fell 3 points among Republicans, 10 among independents and 16 among Democrats. [S10]
- In the June drop, overall approval fell 7 points among Republicans and independents and 9 among Democrats. [S4]
- Gallup's last pre-election poll showed a 92-point party gap in approval (95% of Republicans, 3% of Democrats). [S1]
- I found no 2020 Gallup breakdown by sex, nativity or region. The only subgroup figures I found are for Trump's second term. They show higher early-2020 support among White adults (57%) and women (42%) than he has now. [S6]

**Gallup's own reading.** Gallup said that 46% was still short of the 50% threshold historically associated with incumbents winning a second term. [S5] That threshold is a useful frame for the counterfactual. Before the pandemic Trump was at 49%, and Gallup's averages for that period were his best. Even so, he never reached 50% in any Gallup poll. He is the only president since 1938 without a 50% reading at any point. [S1]

## 2. Analogues

**Incumbents and approval (national)**
- Gallup finds that every incumbent with approval of 50% or higher has won reelection. Those far below 50% have lost. [S21]
- Final pre-election approval: Obama 2012, 52% (won); G.W. Bush 2004, 48% (won); Clinton 1996, 54% (won); G.H.W. Bush 1992, 34% (lost). [S21]
- The two incumbents under 40% lost badly. Carter got 41.0% of the popular vote in 1980 and G.H.W. Bush 37.4% in 1992. [S25]
- On average, an incumbent's vote share has been about 1 point above his final approval. [S25]
- No incumbent under 48% approval before the election has won a second term. [S25]
- Trump's 46% would be roughly in the range of a toss-up or narrow loss, using this rule of thumb. That is my inference from the sources, not a finding of theirs.

**Long low unemployment and steady growth.** I did not find a source that directly tests "long low-unemployment periods". The nearest evidence is Gallup's 2020 economic data and its incumbent record.
- Trump's economic approval of 58% in February matched Clinton's record in October 1996, just before Clinton won in a landslide. [S8]
- Good economic ratings did not translate into overall approval above 50% for Trump. His economic rating averaged about 10 points above his overall approval. [S4]
- That points to polarization limiting any economic bonus. His average approval was 41%, lower than any predecessor's by at least four points. [S1]
- Analogues where a booming economy rescued an incumbent (Clinton 1996, Reagan 1984) had higher baseline approval. Clinton, Reagan, Nixon, Johnson and Eisenhower all had June approval above 50% in their reelection years, with Reagan's 54% the lowest. [S27]

**Years with no major national crisis.** The sources give approval data, not a crisis classification, so I can't cleanly sort years into crisis and non-crisis.
- Of 10 sitting presidents seeking reelection in Gallup's era, 6 won and 3 lost. (This count leaves one out, probably Truman.) [S22]
- The three losers were Ford, Carter and Bush. [S22]
- Across all history, 20 of 34 reelection tries succeeded and 14 failed. [S22]
- Truman is the outlier. Only 39% approved of him in late May or early June 1948, yet he won. [S27]
- Obama in 2012 is the one case of a swing across the line. He rose from 46% in June to 52% before the election, which is the only recorded instance of that kind of recovery. [S25]

**Turnout and voting method in 2020 (the pandemic effect, to subtract in the counterfactual)**
- There were 17 million more voters than in 2016, the largest increase between presidential elections on record. [S14]
- Reported turnout among citizens rose 5 points, to 67%. [S14]
- The EAC counted turnout at 67.7% of CVAP, up 6.7 points. [S17]
- Brookings, using Census data, put 2020 turnout at 66.8%, the highest since 1992. [S20]
- Mail voting was 43% of voters in 2020, against 21% in 2016. Early in-person voting was 26%, against 19%. [S13]
- In all, 69% voted nontraditionally, against about 40% in 2016. [S13]
- Caution on cause: the turnout rise can't be assigned purely to the pandemic. The states with the largest turnout gains tended to be those that made mail voting easy. [S17] That fits with pandemic-era rule changes, but the rise also had campaign intensity and polarization behind it. I found no source that separates these causes.
- In the states using nontraditional methods most, turnout rose 7.7 points. [S13]
- Utah, Hawaii and Texas each rose more than 10 points. [S17]

**By sex**
- Women's turnout was 68% in 2020, against 63% in 2016. Men's was 65%, against 59%. [S14]
- That is +5 points for women and +6 for men.

**By race and ethnicity**
- Turnout rose among non-Hispanic White, Black, Asian and Hispanic citizens. The largest increase was among non-Hispanic Asians. [S14]
- Census gave White non-Hispanic turnout as 71.0% of citizens in 2020 (the table's columns are not fully legible). [S15]
- Brookings found turnout surged among Asian American, Latino and non-college white voters. [S20]
- Asian American voters were the most likely to vote by mail, at 64%. [S18]
- The Census estimates exclude American Indians and Alaska Natives because the sample is too small. [S18] I found no usable figures for that group.

**By region**
- The Northeast went from 6% voting by mail in 2016 to 43% in 2020. [S18]
- Early voting is most popular in Southern states, especially among Black and Hispanic voters. [S18]
- I found no regional vote-share swings. I also found nothing on nativity or citizenship status (naturalized citizens, noncitizens).

**By age and education**
- Turnout among citizens aged 18–34 was 57%, up from 49%. Among those aged 35–64 it was 69%, up from 65%. [S14]

## 3. Named people

The scenario names only the incumbent, Trump, and his 2020 challenger is implied.
- Trump's own pre-pandemic record is covered above. By late July his 41% remained well below the 49% of earlier in the year, when the economy was in good shape and he was enjoying a post-impeachment bounce. [S3]
- Gallup reported that more Americans expected Trump, not Biden, to win (56% to 40% in Sept. 14–28). [S5] This was despite indicators suggesting his reelection was imperiled.
- Biden held a slight edge in favorability, but both men were below 50%. [S5]
- I did not search for Trump's or Biden's statements on specific issues. I can look into that if you want it.

- **Confounded timing.** The June 2020 drop coincided with the Floyd protests, and Trump's January peak followed his impeachment acquittal. The pre-pandem

Questions to answer:
- How have incumbents fared in past elections held during long periods of low unemployment and steady growth?
- How did voters' views of the incumbent change in the 2020 polls before and after the pandemic began?
- How did turnout and the choice of voting method change in 2020 compared with 2016 because of the pandemic?

Evidence by these groups is most useful.
